newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: News of mould in Vietnam coffee crop divides trade.
newsitem.headline: News of mould in Vietnam coffee crop divides trade.

text.p: The extent of mould problems in Vietnam's coffee crop divided Far East coffee dealers on Wednesday while business remains slow because of the gap between Vietnamese export prices and futures in London, traders said.
"It's at a standstill. Nobody wants to buy or sell coffee because of the mould situation in the area," a senior dealer for a European commodity house said.

But a trader for another European dealing house disputed reports that mould is threatening the quality of the coffee crop in Vietnam, the second largest producer of robusta beans in Asia after Indonesia.
"I think what the Vietnamese government said is correct. We have shipped 8,000 tonnes of the new crop recently and we have not found any mould problems," the trader said.
Most of the coffee beans were produced in Dak Lak province, which accounts for two-thirds of the estimated 250,000 tonnes of coffee Vietnam will probably export this year.
Vietnam's state coffee corporation, Vinacafe, slammed on Monday reports that beans from the main producing area of Dak Lak were being hit by mould while urging local producers to focus on quality.
"If a report says the quality is unacceptable, it's wrong," Doan Trieu Nhan, vice-president of Vincafe, told a briefing in Hanoi for traders and journalists.
"A 0.1 to 0.2 percent mould rate is normal, but the report said the percentage was from 3-4 percent," he said, adding that Vietnam had exported some 40,000 tonnes of coffee from its crop so far.
Traders said the weather has cleared up in Dak Lak, which has been plagued by torrential rain from the beginning of the harvest in November.
"What I hear is the weather is fine now," one dealer said.
Earlier problems of excessive moisture in the coffee beans appears to have been resolved, dealers said.
Most of the beans reaching the main southern port of Ho Chi Minh city now have moisture levels of about 12.5-13.0 percent against earlier levels of around 16-17 percent, traders said.
"The coffee is being dried properly," a dealer said. "We're no longer having any problems with moisture."
The trade prefers the coffee beans to have a moisture level not exceeding 13.0 percent.
Regional dealers said that the premium of futures prices in London to export prices in Vietnam was ranging between $200-$400 a tonne.
Vietnam's benchmark Grade 2 coffee was quoted by regional traders at around US$950-$970 a tonne FOB Saigon port against last week's $1,020-$1,050 a tonne FOB from the same port.
LIFFE January robusta coffee futures closed up $28 a tonne at $1,331 on Tuesday.
With prices so low, reports that some farmers were destroying their coffee trees could not be confirmed.
Development of the coffee crop in Indonesia, on the other hand, looks good and dealers were optimistic of a bumper crop when the harvest begins towards the end of the first quarter next year.
"The weather is a bit rainy, but that's good for the coffee," one dealer said.
Indonesia's Grade 4 coffee was priced at around $1,150-$1,200 a tonne FOB Panjang, down slightly from last week's $1,200-$1,250 a tonne, traders said.
Dealers expect London to open $5-$10 higher, mainly on the back of gains in New York.
"It should open up, following the lead of New York," one dealer said.
Trading of the coffee contract in the Singapore Commodity Exchange picked up this week, mainly because of short covering by traders in the city-state, dealers said.
A total of 311 tonnes were sold on Tuesday and 210 tonnes on Monday. The volume in the exchange reach only three tonnes last Friday and nine tonnes on Thursday.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
